newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rumours of reshuffle, elections, grip France.
newsitem.headline: Rumours of reshuffle, elections, grip France.

text.p: France is gripped by rumours that President Jacques Chirac is mulling a cabinet reshuffle or even snap elections, but pollsters said on Wednesday that either could badly backfire for the government.

"An early election would be like Russian roulette," said Pierre Giacometti, director of political studies at the IPSOS polling institute. "It could easily swing the majority to the leftist opposition."

Bringing forward National Assembly elections due in March 1998, to capitalise on a slight upturn in the economy and disarray among the Socialists, might help Chirac secure a new centre-right parliament for the rest of his seven-year term.
The main temptation for a less risky reshuffle is that it could revive Prime Minister Alain Juppe's cabinet in its fight against record unemployment in the run-up to the elections.
But a new team now might look jaded by March.
A growing number of Chirac's prominent allies in parliament have publicly debated the merits of a reshuffle or early elections in recent days -- most say in public they are opposed.

"It's true this is perhaps the time when the president will take an initiative," Pierre Mazeaud, conservative head of the Assembly's legal commission, told Europe 1 radio. "I would rather expect a possible reshuffle. It's true that it's good to change teams."
Juppe said on Wednesday he could not comment on rumours of an early vote or a reshuffle. Last week, he had dismissed speculation about upsetting the calendar.

Opposition far-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said early elections were "probable" as part of a manoeuvre to shield some ministers from possible sleaze probes before they become a campaign issue. He said he had put his campaign staff on a war footing.
Chirac has the power to call elections whenever he wants but has said in the past he has no intention of upsetting the calendar for political reasons.

Another major temptation to go for early elections is to avoid the 1998 election campaign coinciding with wrangling across the European Union about which countries will qualify for a single currency from 1999.
EU debate about which countries meet the strict economic criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty is due in early 1998 on the basis of economic performances in 1997.

"It would be hard to make people swallow early elections. People would feel politicians were trying to confiscate the debate," said Edouard Lecerf, director of political studies at the Louis Harris polling institute.
He said that a reshuffle was far less risky, and could be presented as a more or less technical adjustment to the cabinet.

Philippe Mechet, director of political studies at the Sofres institute, said the government had no obvious bold new project to justify dissolving parliament. That meant it would have to campaign on its record.
"All surveys show that people have a poor opinion of the record, so there is a real danger," he said.

The late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand dissolved the assembly in 1981 and 1988 at the start of his two terms to secure a more favourable parliament. President Charles de Gaulle dissolved parliament in 1962 to secure changes in the political system and in 1968 after the May uprising.

An IPSOS poll at the weekend showed that just 23 percent of people interviewed wanted an early election, against 65 percent against. Other surveys indicate that the Socialists and their allies might well secure most votes.
A reshuffle could help bring back politicians who backed Chirac's former Gaullist ally, then prime minister Edouard Balladur, in a fratricidal battle for the presidency two years ago.

"A reshuffle would have no sense unless there was a major change in policy," said former interior minister Charles Pasqua, who backed Balladur. "I don't believe either in the hypothesis of a reshuffle or dissolution of the Assembly."
